newsitem.title: CHINA: China launches sci-fi meeting with call for change.
newsitem.headline: China launches sci-fi meeting with call for change.

text.p: China opened a world conference on science fiction on Monday with calls for domestic writing to redefine itself as a social and literary force after decades of official repression.

"The development of our nation will depend on scientific education and science fiction is one method of carrying this out," said Zhou Guangzhao, chairman of the China Science and Technology Association (CSTA).
"It is an art form, so the artistic aspect must be improved as well, it should be more literary," Zhou said in a speech at China's 1997 International Conference on Science Fiction.

Chinese science fiction, once the stuff of biting social satire as well as space voyages, is now re-emerging after years of repression by China's communist rulers, who once eyed the forward-looking genre with suspicion.

The breakneck industrialisation that has gripped the country for years has provided fertile ground for science fiction as people seek ways to cope with startling changes, said Yang Xiao, editor of Science Fiction World, the genre's flagship magazine in China.
"Chinese literature has always looked to the past. We have no vanguard literature that looks at the future," Yang said in an interview at the conference.
With 1.2 billion people, China boasts a huge audience for science fiction. Science Fiction World has a circulation of nearly 250,000 -- the biggest readership of any such magazine in the world.

Yang said she hoped domestic science fiction would evolve to resemble its foreign counterparts by developing a more literary style and by playing a positive role in science-related issues such as environmental pollution.
But she made clear readers would not find China's equivalent of George Orwell's famous anti-authoritarian novel "1984" in its pages any time soon.

"I won't publish something that criticises Deng Xiaoping's reforms or that I think is harmful to society," she said, referring to China's late paramount leader who charted the path of market-style economic reform.
Politics may be off-limits to modern writers, but the genre got its start in China with "The City of Cats", a scathing 1933 social novel by revolutionary author Lao She.
Lao was later driven to suicide by ultra-leftist radicals who accused him of betraying the communist cause through his writings.

Science fiction lay dormant until the 1980s, when Beijing relaxed political controls and unleashed a creative wave that sought to deal with where China's ambitious reforms would lead. China's cultural commissars didn't like what they read.
"The fatal blow was delivered in the 1980s when it was decided science fiction was politically, socially and culturally dangerous," said Australian sinologist and literary critic Geremie Barme.
Some science fiction fans are taking matters into their own hands by printing small-circulation magazines that are often far bolder than bigger publications.
In one such magazine, a short story tells of a woman sentenced to die for writing a computer programme that generates "dangerous" words from ancient times.

"I know our life is slipping away. But Kay, I can feel the joy in your eyes, your love, and I am blessed, I am resisting the rules with you. Our gazes fall on that word that gives us a new life together -- freedom," the story concludes.
